candidates.source_name: 1 Enoch (Ethiopian tradition) / Book of the Watchers (1 Enoch 1-36)
candidates.draft_body:
1 Enoch (Ethiopian tradition) Book of the Watchers (1 Enoch 1-36) (c. 200 BC)

'And they took and brought me to a place in which those who were there were like flaming fire, and, when they wished, they appeared as men' — the opening of Enoch's first cosmic journey. The angelic guides who transform between fire-form and man-form establish the Enochic angelological pattern: angels have native fire-existence (their proper-nature mode) but can manifest as men for human communication (their accommodation-mode). The Tewahedo iconographic tradition preserves this dual-mode angelology: angels are depicted in human form in iconographic accommodation, but liturgical-theological references invoke their fire-nature.

candidates.source_name: 1 Enoch (Ethiopian tradition) / Book of the Watchers (1 Enoch 1-36)
candidates.source_attribution: 1 Enoch 17:5, trans. R.H. Charles (1912). PD. Cf. Rev 19:20.
candidates.draft_body:
1 Enoch (Ethiopian tradition) Book of the Watchers (1 Enoch 1-36) (c. 200 BC)

'And I came to the river of fire in which the fire flows like water and discharges itself into the great sea towards the west' — Enoch beholds the river of fire that connects to the cosmic west-sea. The river-of-fire (nahar ʾəsāt) Tewahedo eschatology reads as the eschatological fire that purges + judges; the New Testament's 'lake of fire' (Rev 19:20, 20:10) Tewahedo reads as connected to this Enochic vision. The 'great sea towards the west' is the cosmic-mythic ocean at the world's edge, before which the fire-river ends — establishing the geographical-eschatological boundary of the divine economy.
